To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) learning of smooth and rapid movements can be achieved by using CF spikes as information carriers, (2) learning can be achieved with stochastic models, but not with deterministic models, and (3) the distribution of CF spikes should capture at least the moments of the error signal distribution..

the Poisson model is the only spike model that can achieve cerebellar learning and that efficient cerebellar cerebellar learning requires that the distribution of CF spikes capture the first, second, and third moments of temporal distribution of error.
the stochastic models are essential for efficient learning, and that the Poisson model is sufficient for the OFR and arm movement tasks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what type of information is carried by CF spikes and how the cerebellum can learn to generate smooth and fast movements.
the statistical properties of CF spikes necessary for efficient learning in the cerebellum.
the question of whether the learning can be achieved with the CF spikes, and if so, what are the necessary characteristics of the spike generation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Poisson model is the most appropriate model for the CF spikes for efficient cerebellum learning.
the stochastic models, especially the Poisson model, are more appropriate than the deterministic models for the generation of CF spikes for efficient cerebellum-based learning.
the stochastic models of CF spikes are necessary for efficient learning of cerebellar tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for efficient cerebel-lar learning in a wide range of tasks, the CF spikes must be generated by stochastic mechanisms and the spike-occurrence probability must be a function of the temporal distribution (i.e. first, second and/or third moments) of the error signal.
the stochasticity of CF spike generation is necessary for efficient cerebelar learning.
the Poisson model is the best model for the spike generation in the CF, and the Poisson model can be applied to a wide range of cerebellar motor tasks.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cerebellar learning requires the temporal distribution of the spike occurrences to capture at least the second moment (the variance), which is not captured by the conventional MFRs, and this is the reason why the cerebellar learning is achieved by the stochastic models, such Poisson or gamma models, but is not achieved by the deterministic models.
cerebellar learning is not only possible with CF spikes but also that it requires a certain distribution of CF spike timing, which is different from the conventional MFRs.
cerebellar learning is possible by CF spikes, which is the first theoretical study to demonstrate this possibility.
